OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Long-form reasoning and tool calling traces accumulate errors and stale content that anchor subsequent generations, a phenomenon known as \emph{context rot}. Existing scaffolds mitigate this with \textit{fixed-interval} compaction triggered at a token threshold, but such triggers are blind to trajectory structure and risk discarding partial results mid-derivation or mid-search. Both are needed. The tool alone is unevenly used across open-weight models, often invoked at unhelpful moments or not at all; the rubric alone cannot act. Together, they elicit effective adaptive compaction without any fine-tuning. On competition math (IMO-Answerbench, HMMT Nov 25 / Feb 26) with four Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 models and agentic search (BrowseComp, BrowseComp-Plus) with three deployed agents, \method{} matches or exceeds fixed-interval summarization at a fraction of the token cost, improving over a no-summarization baseline by up to 16.7 points on math and 5--9 points on agentic search at 30--70\% lower per-question cost. OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: CoSER: Coordinating LLM-Based Persona Simulation of Established Roles
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Role-playing language agents (RPLAs) have emerged as promising applications of large language models (LLMs). However, simulating established characters presents a challenging task for RPLAs, due to the lack of authentic character datasets and nuanced evaluation methods using such data. In this paper, we present CoSER, a collection of a high-quality dataset, open models, and an evaluation protocol towards effective RPLAs of established characters. The CoSER dataset covers 17,966 characters from 771 renowned books. It provides authentic dialogues with real-world intricacies, as well as diverse data types such as character experiences and internal thoughts. Drawing from acting methodology, we introduce given-circumstance acting for training and evaluating role-playing LLMs, where LLMs sequentially portray multiple characters in book scenes. Using our dataset, we develop CoSER 8B and CoSER 70B, i.e., advanced open role-playing LLMs built on LLaMA-3.1 models. Extensive experiments demonstrate the value of the CoSER dataset for RPLA training, evaluation and retrieval. Moreover, CoSER 70B exhibits state-of-the-art performance surpassing or matching GPT-4o on our evaluation and three existing benchmarks, i.e., achieving 75.80% and 93.47% accuracy on the InCharacter and LifeChoice benchmarks respectively. Our code, dataset and models are available at: https://github.com/Neph0s/CoSER.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.23342.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
arXiv|arxiv:2611.23342.abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.07374.title: Multigroup Fairness and Omniprediction: Separations and Equivalences
arXiv|arxiv:2610.07374.abstract: Omniprediction is a learning guarantee which requires a single predictor to be competitive relative to the best hypothesis from a benchmark class for any loss chosen from a family of loss functions. Loss Outcome Indistinguishability (loss OI for short) is a stronger notion that implies omniprediction. It requires the predicted distribution on labels to be indistinguishable from the true distribution to tests that depend on the loss functions and the benchmark class. Multiaccuracy and multicalibration are multigroup fairness notions that generalize classical notions of calibration and accuracy in expectation. Most known learning algorithms for omniprediction (both for the standard notion and for strengthenings like loss OI) rely on some version of these multigroup fairness notions, or on an intermediate notion called calibrated multiaccuracy. We ask if this is necessary: Does omniprediction require some form of multigroup fairness? We show that the answer is no for (plain) omniprediction, and yes for loss OI. First, a sequence of works shows that multicalibration or calibrated multiaccuracy imply omniprediction. We rule out even a weak converse, by showing that omniprediction for proper losses does not imply even accuracy in expectation, a much weaker notion than any of calibration, multiaccuracy, or multicalibration. Second, prior work showed how to achieve loss OI from a combination of calibration and multiaccuracy. We show a converse: loss OI is equivalent to a form of calibrated multiaccuracy.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: SciCoQA: Quality Assurance for Scientific Paper–Code Alignment
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Discrepancies between scientific papers and their code undermine reproducibility, a concern that grows as automated research agents scale scientific output beyond human review capacity. Whether LLMs can reliably detect such discrepancies has not been systematically measured. To this end, we present SciCoQA, a dataset of 635 paper-code discrepancies (92 real, 543 synthetic) for this cross-modal verification task. Across 22 evaluated models, even the best-performing LLMs, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5 Mini, detect only 46.7% of real-world discrepancies, revealing a critical gap in automated scientific quality assurance. We construct SciCoQA from GitHub issues and reproducibility papers, and propose a synthetic generation pipeline to scale beyond AI to Physics, Quantitative Biology, and other computational sciences. We further introduce a taxonomy of discrepancy types and categories to characterize the occurring mismatches. Our analysis shows that models particularly struggle with omitted paper details, long-context inputs, and papers outside their pre-training corpus.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.25796.title: Fair Regression under Approximate Demographic Parity
arXiv|arxiv:2610.25796.abstract: Exact demographic parity requires the same prediction distribution across sensitive groups. In regression, this can be too restrictive and reduce predictive accuracy. We instead bound every pairwise Wasserstein distance between group-specific prediction distributions by a chosen tolerance, allowing the groups to differ while keeping fairness tunable. On the real line, the prediction and constrained transport problems have the same infimum. If the transport problem attains this value and suitable Monge maps exist, a deterministic transport-form predictor realizes it. Under a standard one-dimensional condition, the problem becomes a bounded quantile optimization that is convex when the conditional expected loss is convex in prediction. Under squared loss with two positively weighted groups, the $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_\infty$ constraints yield soft-thresholding, shrinkage, and clipping. Under the stated conditions, we establish rates for the known-cost plug-in estimator. When the cost is unavailable, we describe an observed-loss computational proxy. Synthetic and California 2018 ACS studies illustrate the tunable fairness-accuracy trade-off and distinguish calibration feasibility from held-out fairness and accuracy.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.31903.title: Choir: An Open Protocol for Distributed Multi-Agent Autoformalization
arXiv|arxiv:2609.31903.abstract: AI agents can now formalize entire textbooks and major theorems in proof assistants such as Lean, but current efforts are typically centralized: a single team runs all agents and bears the full computational cost. We introduce Choir, an open protocol for distributed formalization. Choir decomposes a project into tasks that can be completed by independent contributors, each running their own agent with their own LLM subscription, while coordinating entirely through the project's GitHub repository. To support open participation, every contribution is checked by a deterministic gate before merge. Choir supports Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq, and is open source and modular, allowing projects to replace individual components or extend the protocol.

arXiv|arxiv:2602.24195.title: Uncertainty Quantification for Multimodal Large Language Models with Incoherence-adjusted Semantic Volume
arXiv|arxiv:2602.24195.abstract: Despite their capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) may produce plausible but erroneous outputs, hindering reliable deployment. Accurate uncertainty metrics could enable escalation of unreliable queries to human experts or larger models for improved performance. However, existing uncertainty metrics have practical constraints, such as being designed only for specific modalities, reliant on external tools, or computationally expensive. We introduce UMPIRE, a training-free uncertainty quantification framework for MLLMs that works efficiently across various input and output modalities without external tools, relying only on the models' own internal modality features. Inspired by Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs), UMPIRE computes a novel incoherence-adjusted semantic volume of sampled MLLM responses for a given task instance, which couples semantic embedding dispersion with the quadratic entropy of the responses. This approach effectively captures both the global semantic diversity of samples and the local incoherence of responses based on internal model confidence. We provide theoretical analysis motivating UMPIRE's design, and extensive experiments show that UMPIRE consistently outperforms baseline metrics in error detection and uncertainty calibration across image, audio, and video-text benchmarks, even with small sample budgets. We also demonstrate UMPIRE's generalization to non-text output tasks, including image and audio generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/daohieu17ctt/UMPIRE.

arXiv|arxiv:2607.22305.title: A Roadmap to Impactful Pluralistic Alignment Research
arXiv|arxiv:2607.22305.abstract: Much research on responsible AI aims to change the behavior of AI systems that billions of people use. Pluralistic value alignment---the goal of building AI systems that represent and serve diverse human values and perspectives---has emerged as one such active research agenda. Yet, in an audit of the major frontier labs and open-weight developers, we find no public evidence that it has shaped how their models are trained or evaluated. Pluralistic alignment requires adoption to achieve its main goals, so we identify three barriers and lay out a roadmap of research to address each: 1. The justifications for pluralistic alignment so far are mostly normative or theoretical. Studies are needed that measure the benefits and drawbacks of pluralistic AI for users and society. 2. The pluralistic alignment research community has not settled when pluralistic behavior is warranted or what it should look like in practice. Research is needed to specify this behavior concretely enough for developers to operationalize. 3. Existing pluralism evaluations and methods are not ready for deployment. Evaluations and methods are needed that report their effects on other model properties and meet the requirements of production systems. These barriers are not unique to pluralistic alignment, so our roadmap applies to other areas of responsible AI research with similar theories of change. As people hand more decisions to AI systems and AI agents act on their behalf, we hope our roadmap helps this research reach the deployed models making those decisions.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: When New Generators Arrive: Lifelong Machine-Generated Text Attribution via Ridge Feature Transfer
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Machine-generated text (MGT) attribution aims to identify the specific generator responsible for a given text, thereby providing fine-grained evidence for model accountability and misuse investigation. As new large language models continue to emerge, attribution models must continuously incorporate new generators while preserving their ability to recognize previously seen ones. Prior works have shown that this lifelong MGT attribution setting is challenging, and existing methods often struggle to achieve a stable balance between adapting to new classes and retaining old ones. To address this issue, we propose RidgeFT, a lightweight analytic update framework that does not rely on exemplar replay. RidgeFT trains a task-aware encoder on the initial generator set, stores compact class-wise sufficient statistics when each generator class is first observed, and then freezes the encoder for replay-free closed-form updates. It then suppresses generator-irrelevant variation through covariance calibration, improves representation capacity with fixed random features, and updates new classes through closed-form ridge regression based on class-level sufficient statistics. Across multi-topic evaluations with varying initial generator setups, consistently outperforms baselines. It achieves the best overall macro-F1 across domains, backbones, and incremental protocols, while also improving both old-class retention and new-class adaptation. These results suggest that feature-stable analytic updates provide a simple yet effective approach to lifelong MGT attribution.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: MCU: An Evaluation Framework for Open-Ended Game Agents
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Developing AI agents capable of interacting with open-world environments to solve diverse tasks is a compelling challenge. However, evaluating such open-ended agents remains difficult, with current benchmarks facing scalability limitations. To address this, we introduce \textit{Minecraft Universe} (MCU), a comprehensive evaluation framework set within the open-world video game Minecraft. MCU incorporates three key components: (1) an expanding collection of 3,452 composable atomic tasks that encompasses 11 major categories and 41 subcategories of challenges; (2) a task composition mechanism capable of generating infinite diverse tasks with varying difficulty; and (3) a general evaluation framework that achieves 91.5\% alignment with human ratings for open-ended task assessment. Empirical results reveal that even state-of-the-art foundation agents struggle with the increasing diversity and complexity of tasks. These findings highlight the necessity of MCU as a robust benchmark to drive progress in AI agent development within open-ended environments. Our evaluation code and scripts are available at https://github.com/CraftJarvis/MCU.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.11754.title: What Output-Only Review Cannot Verify: Study Contracts for Research Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2610.11754.abstract: Some defects in an AI-generated study can be identified from its artifacts; others require knowledge of what was approved before execution. We propose study contracts that bind declared experimental choices, run obligations and claim scope to recorded execution evidence, and distinguish this contract-relative verification from scientific truth. A diagnostic using eight self-authored clean/mutated pairs illustrates the information boundary. A deterministic checker applying a registered, fault-specific rule to approved and executed objects detected all eight registered mutations. Across eighteen recorded judge aliases given individual metadata-filtered packages without pair context or the registry-selected fault label, 104 of 144 mutated evaluation cases received defect flags; the remaining cases comprised 32 abstentions and eight terminal failures, with no explicit clean decisions on mutated cases. Some packages retained approval and execution fields, including digests. The prompt instructed judges to abstain when evidence was insufficient. These results characterize a deliberately information-asymmetric development setting; they do not isolate the effect of authoritative information from differences in task specification and rule selection, and they are not comparative verifier quality or agent reward hacking. We identify full-information comparisons, legitimate-adaptation controls and closed-loop agent evaluations as necessary tests of whether contract checks improve useful compliant completion under optimization.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is commonly done via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or, more simply, via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We propose TUR-DPO, a topology- and uncertainty-aware variant of DPO that rewards how answers are derived, not only what they say, by eliciting lightweight reasoning topologies and combining semantic faithfulness, utility, and topology quality into a calibrated uncertainty signal. Empirically, across open 7–8B models and benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, factual question answering, summarization, and helpful/harmless dialogue, TUR-DPO improves judge win-rates, faithfulness, and calibration relative to DPO while preserving training simplicity and avoiding online rollouts. arXiv|arxiv:2602.03665.title: MM-SCALE: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Moral Judgment in Vision-Language Models
arXiv|arxiv:2602.03665.abstract: Vision-Language Models increasingly make socially consequential judgments from image-text inputs, yet current evaluations often stop at verdict-level accuracy: whether the final label is human-aligned, not whether it follows from the correct evidence. We introduce MM-SCALE (Multimodal Moral SCALE), a benchmark for evidence-grounded moral judgment built around a design choice: each image is paired with multiple action scenarios, so models must compare how different actions interact with the same visual context rather than score images in isolation. MM-SCALE contains 8,444 image contexts and 21,977 action scenarios, each annotated with a 5-point moral acceptability rating and a modality-grounding label indicating whether the human judgment relied on text, image, or both. Three tasks evaluate whether models (i) assign calibrated scalar moral scores, (ii) preserve human orderings within a shared visual context, and (iii) ground rationales in the evidence source humans found critical to judgment. Across models, aggregate metrics overstate alignment: NDCG@5 remains high across models, while within-image pairwise accuracy remains only 0.53-0.62 even on scenario pairs whose human mean ratings differ by at least one point. CoT has inconsistent effects on calibration and does not reliably improve within-image ordering. Evidence grounding evaluations further show that models often describe visual context without making it critical for the verdict. These results reveal an evidence-grounding failure in current VLMs and position MM-SCALE as an evaluation testbed for moral judgment under shared image contexts. This dataset includes potentially harmful and sensitive visual content. Images are intended solely for evaluation.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Scientific research proceeds through iterative cycles of hypothesis generation, experiment design, execution, and revision. AI agents can automate parts of this process, but existing approaches typically follow a single research trajectory or coordinate through a central planner with fixed objectives. As a result, they struggle to sustain parallel exploration, adapt as experimental evidence changes, or preserve knowledge of failed directions over long-running experiments. We introduce AutoScientists, a decentralized team of AI agents for long-running computational scientific experimentation. Agents interpret a shared experimental state, self-organize into teams around promising hypotheses, critique proposals before using experimental compute, and share successes and failures to reduce redundant exploration. Under matched experimental budgets, AutoScientists improves over prior AI agents across biomedical machine learning, language model training optimization, and protein fitness prediction. On BioML-Bench, spanning biomedical imaging, protein engineering, single-cell omics, and drug discovery, AutoScientists achieves a mean leaderboard percentile of 74.4% across 24 tasks, improving over the strongest AI agent by +8.33% in the absolute leaderboard percentile points. On GPT training optimization, AutoScientists reaches a target validation bits-per-byte 1.9$\times$ faster than Autoresearch and continues discovering improvements from a starting champion where the single-agent approach finds none (7 vs. 0 accepted improvements). On ProteinGym fitness prediction, AutoScientists discovers a method for ACE2-Spike binding that improves over the current state-of-the-art model by +12.5% in Spearman correlation. Applied without modification across all 217 ProteinGym assays, the same method improves over the prior state of the art by +6.5% (Spearman correlation).

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: AdvEvo-MARL: Shaping Internalized Safety through Adversarial Co-Evolution in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems excel at planning, tool use, and role coordination, but their openness and interaction complexity also expose them to jailbreak and adversarial collaboration. Existing defenses fall into two lines: (i) self-verification that asks each agent to pre-filter unsafe instructions before execution, and (ii) external guard modules that police behaviors. The former often underperforms because a standalone agent lacks sufficient capacity to detect cross-agent unsafe chains and delegation-induced risks; the latter increases system overhead and creates a single-point-of-failure—once compromised, system-wide safety collapses, and adding more guards worsens cost and complexity. To solve these challenges, we propose AdvEvo-MARL, a co-evolutionary multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that internalizes safety into task agents. Rather than relying on external guards, AdvEvo-MARL jointly optimizes attackers (which synthesize evolving jailbreak prompts) and defenders (task agents trained to both accomplish their duties and resist attacks) in adversarial learning environments. To stabilize learning and foster cooperation, we introduce a public baseline for advantage estimation: agents within the same functional group share a group-level mean-return baseline, enabling lower-variance updates and stronger intra-group coordination. Across representative attack scenarios, AdvEvo-MARL consistently keeps attack-success rate (ASR) below 20\%, whereas baselines reach up to 38.33\%, while preserving or even improving task accuracy (up to +3.67\%). These results show that safety and utility can be jointly improved without relying on extra guard agents or added system overhead.

CVF|https://openaccess.thecvf.com/conten.title: SpaceTools: Tool-Augmented Spatial Reasoning via Double Interactive RL
CVF|https://openaccess.thecvf.com/conten.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate strong qualitative visual understanding, but struggle with metrically precise spatial reasoning required for embodied applications. The agentic paradigm promises that VLMs can use a wide variety of tools that could augment these capabilities, such as depth estimators, segmentation models, and pose estimators. Yet it remains an open challenge how to realize this vision without solely relying on handcrafted prompting strategies or enforcing fixed, predefined tool pipelines that limit VLMs' ability to discover optimal tool-use patterns. Reinforcement Learning could overcome this gap, but has so far been limited to reasoning with a single visual tool due to the large search space in multi-tool reasoning. In the teaching phase, we combine demonstrations from a single tool specialist trained via interactive RL with traces from a frontier model using all tools. In the exploration phase, the model further refines multi-tool coordination through continued RL. Our model, SpaceTools, with tool-augmented spatial reasoning ability, achieves state-of-the-art performance on spatial understanding benchmarks (RoboSpatial-Home, BLINK, Internal Benchmark) and demonstrates reliable real-world manipulation using a 7-DOF robot as a tool. DIRL provides substantial improvements over the vanilla SFT (+12% on RoboSpatial) and RL (+16% on RoboSpatial) baselines. Project page: https://spacetools.github.io/.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.05107.abstract: Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.00247.title: Taurus: LLM-in-the-Loop CT Annotation Matches Coding Agents at Half the Cost
arXiv|arxiv:2611.00247.abstract: Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes. In the first version of Taurus, the model's review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than the noise between two reviews of the same case. A free-form agent running Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher on most datasets. Moving what the free-form agents did well into the automated pass then carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version smooths the label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for the large errors the automated pass tends to make, such as an aneurysm drawn to half its size. Each check that fires puts a multiple-choice question to the model, with candidate corrections drawn on the scan. It matched the surface smoothness of the human references, and in the primary metric we found no difference from the free-form Opus agent, at under half its cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case. Most of what made Taurus competitive came from the harness and its automation rather than from the language model itself. Taurus shows that this kind of annotation can be automated, so that expert time can move from drawing labels to checking them.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: In this paper, we aim to establish a simple, effective, and theoretically grounded benchmark for rigorously probing abstract reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Based on this framework, we introduce two novel complementary metrics: Γ measures basic reasoning accuracy, while ∆ quantifies a model's reliance on specific symbols rather than underlying patterns - a key indicator of true abstraction versus mere memorization. Science Advances|https://doi.org/10.1126.title: Machine psychology for language models
Science Advances|https://doi.org/10.1126.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.33633.title: ProbeID: Verifying MCP Tool Identity for LLM Agents under Registry Drift
arXiv|arxiv:2610.33633.abstract: Agents select tools by copyable descriptions, which cannot establish which implementation runs. ProbeID compares canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes with a trusted admission reference and abstains on ambiguity, so a squatter must copy probe-observable behavior. With the gold present, independent probes and a fixed margin, standard concentration arguments give a shared probe budget logarithmic in the candidate count and bound the joint probability of a wrong decision. On cached MCP-IdentityDrift cases, strict choice reaches \(0.956\) hit@1 while description routers fall near chance, but simpler exact comparisons tie it, MMD better tolerates heavy value noise, and a 32B behavioral judge is similarly accurate at higher cost. Random probes from agent banks and a prospective held-out study of 38 tools test theory-set thresholds. On the agent banks, equality refuses every reachable replacement from 64 probes and the bounded distance from 512, and sharper post hoc gates halve both. Over eleven weeks, 7 of 59 real tools changed responses despite version pins. Verification depends on reference integrity, probe coverage, and response noise.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.37353.title: Cost-based variable selection for prediction models
arXiv|arxiv:2610.37353.abstract: Objective: Variable selection for clinical prediction models is commonly done on statistical grounds related to model fit. Statistical approaches ignore the cost of misclassifications and the harm of measuring a variable. We aim to develop a decision-analytic variable selection algorithm based on net benefit. Materials and Methods: The proposed algorithm selects the set of predictors by exhaustively comparing the net benefit of all combinations using cross validation, with an extension based on backward elimination for settings with many predictors. Variables are selected if the increased net benefit from better predictiveness exceeds the net benefit reduction from the harm of variable measurement. Harm includes financial expense, time, resource allocation, and patient burden. We illustrate the algorithm through a simulated example and three real case studies. We compare its performance to traditional backward elimination and LASSO. Results: Across the case studies, parsimonious models were generated that optimized clinical utility with minimal impact on discrimination and calibration. Penalizing predictors based on their cost ensured that expensive or burdensome variables were only selected if they offer sufficient clinical utility. The algorithm was implemented in the R package NBvarsel. Discussion: Decision-analytic variable selection allows prediction models to maximize patient benefit while minimizing unnecessary clinical burden and costs. Conclusion: Clinical utility should not be an afterthought reserved only for implementation. By integrating a harm-adjusted net benefit metric directly into the variable selection process, NBvarsel allows researchers to select only the variables that sufficiently improve clinical utility.

arXiv|arxiv:2604.07789.title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2604.07789.abstract: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.10151.title: WorldMind: Test-Time Scaling for Visual Spatial Reasoning through Latent World Simulation
arXiv|arxiv:2611.10151.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v337/.title: Efficient Confidence Set Enumeration for Multi-label Conformal Classification
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v337/.abstract: Conformal prediction is a distribution-free and model agnostic framework that can provide statistical guarantees to machine learning algorithms: a point-wise predictor is transformed into a conformal predictor that outputs sets of predictions which include the ground truth with a user defined confidence rate. In multi-label conformal classification however, the exponential growth of the output space makes confidence sets prohibitively complex to compute in the general case. In this paper, we analyze this challenge under the prism of enumeration complexity. We detail a general approach for confidence set enumeration based on the flashlight method, prove a sufficient condition for efficient enumeration and apply this method on three types of problems. First, we give an enumeration algorithm with linear delay for modular non-conformity losses. Then, we discuss informed conformal classification where a boolean circuit specifies a set of valid label combinations and prove a sufficient condition for efficient enumeration based on standard properties of the circuit. Moreover, we leverage our results on informed conformal classification to tackle label interactions in the loss. Finally, we illustrate the benefits of our approach with a few experiments.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.09025.title: SPIN: Shadow Predictive Indexer for Sparse Attention
arXiv|arxiv:2610.09025.abstract: Indexer-based sparse attention reduces the cost of core attention by passing only a fixed, small number of important tokens to it. However, the indexer must still score the entire KV cache at every decoding step. This scoring overhead becomes a major bottleneck as the context length grows. We propose SPIN (Shadow Predictive Indexer) to reduce this indexer overhead. SPIN uses lightweight, history-based prediction to identify important KV blocks, avoiding the need to score the full KV cache at every decoding step. SPIN keeps the score history fresh with random exploration and allocates the block budget across layers by their measured miss rates. SPIN treats KV blocks and speculative decoding as first-class design and implementation considerations. Across extensive evaluations on long-context and agentic benchmarks, SPIN achieves 30-40% sparsity while preserving task quality. With larger exploration shares and per-layer block budgets, SPIN keeps task quality on the especially difficult MRCRv2 benchmark close to baseline at 50-57% effective block sparsity. In end-to-end vLLM serving, SPIN improves output throughput by up to 13.9% and reduces median inter-token latency by up to 13.6%.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.37522.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains compact language agents with teacher feedback on student-generated trajectories. In multi-turn tasks, compounding errors can move students beyond the teacher's effective supervision. arXiv|arxiv:2611.02102.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
arXiv|arxiv:2611.02102.abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.04233.title: Neyman-Pearson Classification with Indecisions: Simultaneous Control of Selective Type I and Type II Errors
arXiv|arxiv:2610.04233.abstract: Binary classification often requires controlling both type I and type II error rates at prespecified levels. When the class distributions overlap substantially, the two error limits may be incompatible if every observation must be classified. We study Neyman-Pearson classification with indecisions (NPI), which permits uncertain observations to remain unclassified and assesses selective type I and type II errors among definitive classifications within each class. For an independently trained score, we develop a model-free calibration procedure that combines all candidate threshold pairs passing calibration into a rule whose decision region contains that of every passing candidate. We couple the entire threshold search to a common martingale within each class and compute its finite-horizon crossing probability exactly, avoiding a multiplicity adjustment for the number of candidate pairs. The resulting classifier satisfies both population selective error limits simultaneously with user-specified high probability in finite samples, without assumptions on the accuracy of the fitted score. We bound the additional indecision due to calibration and evaluate the procedure in simulations and applications to recidivism and credit-default prediction.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.21488.abstract: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.15456.title: Bet Imaginatively, not Historically in Independent-Data Sequential Testing
arXiv|arxiv:2611.15456.abstract: Sequential testing avoids some of the many controversies and drawbacks related to traditional batch testing with p-values. In particular, the testing by betting paradigm has developed rapidly in recent years; it frames the level of evidence against the null as the wealth of a player in a betting game. Naturally, how much a player should bet is a key consideration, and should reflect their confidence in what they know about the next observed data point. Much current work uses standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems. In the stochastic setting, where the observed data is independent and stationary, these approaches may be suboptimal. We propose a simple betting strategy, follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE), that exploits the i.i.d. nature of a data stream to estimate the e-power of our current test on the underlying distribution. We average not over the historical evidence collected so far, as generic online learning-based methods do, but instead over the equally-likely possible data sequences we might have seen based on shuffling the data. With an additional principled regularization technique, this simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.01110.title: How Much Can Language Models Gain from Test-Time Computation?
arXiv|arxiv:2610.01110.abstract: How much can test-time computation improve a language model, and at what cost? Test-time scaling is widely proposed as a substitute for larger models, but existing comparisons mostly evaluate one domain at a time and rarely charge selection to the budget. We introduce SELF-POT, a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures the test-time potential of a model across competition mathematics, competitive programming, and agentic workflows. SELF-POT separates candidate coverage from final accuracy on static tasks, tracks correctness transitions under revision, and measures protocol completion alongside task success in agentic environments. Under a unified budget rule, it compares Direct inference with parallel sampling and self-revision under fixed multiples of the Direct budget, and charges every model call, including selection and critique, in dollars. This design supports two kinds of comparison: the gain a model obtains from additional inference, and a lower-cost model with additional inference against a stronger model. Across five low-cost reasoning models on 350 sealed tasks, with Claude Opus 5.5 Direct as the reference, the returns depend on the domain, the selection rule, and failure handling. When we replay the retained programming candidate pools, public-example selection raises correct submissions from 376 to 453 of 500 scheduled cells while saving 12-49% of logical API cost across models, and simply retaining an available candidate when judging fails recovers 61 submissions at unchanged cost. On identical mathematics pools, judging with fallback yields 186 correct submissions versus 182 for voting, while voting saves 12-21% of logical API cost. These controlled replays show how selection and failure handling change the gains realized from the same generated candidates, and they quantify the marginal value of a model judge.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.05171.title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
arXiv|arxiv:2611.05171.abstract: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $μ$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

arXiv|arxiv:2506.22992.title: MARBLE: An Agentic Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning and Visual Abstraction
arXiv|arxiv:2506.22992.abstract: A central challenge for multimodal language models (MLLMs) in real-world tasks is to abstract visual observations into structured spatial states and reason over how those states change under actions over long horizons. Existing multimodal benchmarks often focus on static question answering, where answers can be directly extracted from images, or assume symbolic states are available and bypass the visual-to-spatial abstraction process. We present MARBLE, a diagnostic benchmark for spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning across three agent environments: CUBE, MAZE, and BLOX. MARBLE spans 2D and 3D spatial puzzles under geometric constraints, dynamic layouts, and spatial transformations, with difficulty systematically controlled along two axes: observation format and planning horizon. Extensive evaluations show that frontier MLLMs struggle on MARBLE, with the strongest model GPT-5.4 achieving only a 7.3% average success rate across the three environments in the hardest setting. Pairwise ablations on the open-weight models identify visual-to-spatial abstraction as the major bottleneck: when models must infer spatial states from images instead of receiving human-annotated states, success drops from 50.7% to 3.7% for Gemma-4-31B and from 87.9% to 6.5% for Kimi-K2.6. The results indicate that models often fail to construct precise spatial states from visual observations before planning, a task that is straightforward for humans. Overall, MARBLE reveals the gap in reliable visual-to-spatial abstraction for frontier MLLMs and provides a controlled testbed for measuring progress in spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.22115.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
arXiv|arxiv:2611.22115.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

arXiv|arxiv:2608.30976.title: CastClaw: A Human-in-the-Loop Autonomous Agent for Interactive Time Series Forecasting
arXiv|arxiv:2608.30976.abstract: Practical time-series forecasting requires domain knowledge, constraints, plausibility checks, and human intervention. We present CastClaw, an interactive forecasting system centered on an autonomous forecasting loop and supported by a forecasting-oriented harness. Users create and refine tasks in natural language through command-line and Web interfaces. An internal large language model (LLM) agent reads the task and evidence, selects a permitted tool action or request for human feedback, and uses checked results to decide whether to continue, revisit an analysis, switch a candidate, or stop. The harness supplies tool integration, controlled execution, state management, historical validation, and execution limits. npm distribution connects installation and configuration to interactive execution and forecast and report export. Across five public electricity-price datasets, CastClaw achieves the lowest point-estimate MSE and MAE among 16 baselines. A Nord Pool case study illustrates its inspectable decision process, while provincial electricity-load data from North China (January--June 2026) demonstrate offline task execution.

arXiv|arxiv:2310.17882.title: LOOP-MAC: Learning-Based Multi-Agent Coordination with Guaranteed Local Feasibility in a Virtual Power Plant
arXiv|arxiv:2310.17882.abstract: By aggregating distributed energy resources (DERs) into a single dispatchable resource, virtual power plants (VPPs) enable the grid to use the flexibility of numerous small-scale DERs. Delivering an aggregate VPP commitment requires multi-agent coordination, where agents manage local DER models and operating constraints while jointly meeting a power commitment within limited communication rounds. Classical distributed optimization is computationally intensive, requiring iterative local optimization and repeated communication to reach consensus. Learning-based methods can accelerate coordination but often lack guarantees of local feasibility and accurate commitment tracking. This paper proposes LOOP-MAC (Learning to Optimize the Optimization Process for Multi-Agent Coordination), a fully decentralized learning-based framework that ensures local feasibility by construction while efficiently reducing the aggregate commitment gap. LOOP-MAC employs a two-stage decision process. Learned coordination uses neural optimizers equipped with a gauge layer to produce locally feasible schedules through a few rounds of message exchange. Local adjustment then rebalances each schedule toward feasible flexibility extremes using a commitment-gap estimate inferred from messages already received. The adjusted schedule remains locally feasible as a convex combination of feasible schedules, and the adjustment requires no additional communication round. On a 100-agent VPP, five communication rounds followed by local adjustment reduce the mean commitment gap from 5.1% to 0.75% of the agents' aggregate absolute power and the optimality gap from 3.93% to 3.07% relative to learned coordination alone. Per-agent online computation takes approximately 1.1 ms, including the adjustment.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.33118.title: The Paired Thermal Channel Is Two Orthogonal Axes: A Controlled Attribution Study of Calibration Cost and Detection Gain in Infrared Person Detection
arXiv|arxiv:2610.33118.abstract: The calibrated thermal channel in infrared person detection comprises two structurally orthogonal axes. True calibrated $ΔT$ outperforms scale-matched grayscale pseudo-$ΔT$ by $+0.0221$ mAP (paired Wilcoxon $p=0.0098$, Cohen's $d=+1.08$), confirming that the calibrated channel carries information the grayscale channel lacks. The calibration axis is driven by the joint pairing-scale condition. Preserving both paired correspondence and absolute calibrated scale raises expected calibration error (ECE) from $\approx 0.05$ to $0.142$. The $2\times 2$ interaction ($p=0.0059$) localizes the rise to this condition. Breaking either factor alone returns ECE to the broken-factor level (true-vs-const $p=0.002$; true-vs-shuffled $p=0.002$). Under post-hoc temperature scaling, the pairing cost survives recalibration ($p=0.002$), while the scale cost is largely absorbed ($p=0.16$). As regards the detection axis, the gain stems from structural de-structuring. Phase randomization, which destroys spatial structure while preserving per-sample variance, yields $+0.0185$ mAP over true $ΔT$ on FLIR ADAS ($p=0.014$, $d=+0.96$). The FLAME~3 gain is $+0.0064$ mAP ($p=0.078$, n=8). On the calibration axis, the same intervention is insignificant on FLIR ADAS ($p=0.47$) but significant on FLAME~3 ($p=0.0078$). These findings rest on a five-arm controlled attribution with temperature-evidential learning (TEL) as the testbed. TEL obtains a single evidence-derived routing scalar together with a complementary diagnostic entropy, and establishes a finite-evidence degeneracy theorem proving that the acquisition product degenerates to this scalar with a closed-form bound. A physical $0.5^\circ$C threshold admits cross-dataset physical readings, whereas a gray threshold of $20$ inverts without physical interpretation.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: $\texttt{BetaConform}$: Efficient MAP Estimation of LLM Ensemble Judgment Performance with Prior Transfer
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: LLM ensembles are widely used for LLM judges. However, how to estimate their accuracy, especially in an efficient way, is unknown. In this paper, we present a principled $\textit{maximum a posteriori}$ (MAP) framework for an economical and precise estimation of the performance of LLM ensemble judgment. arXiv|arxiv:2609.22774.abstract: This paper presents our system for Track 2 of the NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 10 on citation-level faithfulness in AI-assisted scientific reporting. Given an atomic scientific claim and the structured full text of its cited paper, the task requires both a four-way relation label and up to three evidence paragraph identifiers. The label head ensembles a paragraph-aware cross-encoder with a document-level DeBERTa-large classifier, followed by class-wise decision calibration. Probability-level fusion is motivated by an out-of-fold tendency to over-predict Topical Match. The evidence head combines paragraph scores from top-20 and top-30 joint models with BM25 scores. Ablations and error analysis show that model complementarity and calibration drive the label gains. Gold-evidence inference changes label Macro-F1 negligibly, whereas evidence ranking remains important for Joint@3.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.19202.title: Omni-Workspace: Benchmarking Omni-Modal AI Assistants on Multimodal Workspace Tasks
arXiv|arxiv:2611.19202.abstract: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.23438.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
arXiv|arxiv:2610.23438.abstract: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing $\textbf{225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Effective social intelligence simulation requires language agents to dynamically adjust reasoning depth, a capability notably absent in current studies. arXiv|arxiv:2509.11337.title: On the Escaping Efficiency of Distributed Adversarial Training Algorithms
arXiv|arxiv:2509.11337.abstract: Adversarial training has been widely studied in recent years due to its role in improving model robustness against adversarial attacks. This paper focuses on comparing different distributed adversarial training algorithms--including centralized and decentralized strategies--within multi-agent learning environments. Previous studies have highlighted the importance of model flatness in determining robustness. To this end, we develop a general theoretical framework to study the escaping efficiency of these algorithms from local minima, which is closely related to the flatness of the resulting models. We show that when the perturbation bound is sufficiently small (i.e., when the attack strength is relatively mild) and a large batch size is used, decentralized adversarial training algorithms--including consensus and diffusion--are guaranteed to escape faster from local minima than the centralized strategy, thereby favoring flatter minima. However, as the perturbation bound increases, this trend may no longer hold. In the simulation results, we illustrate our theoretical findings and systematically compare the performance of models obtained through decentralized and centralized adversarial training algorithms. The results highlight the potential of decentralized strategies to enhance the robustness of models in distributed settings.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.00583.title: Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams
arXiv|arxiv:2610.00583.abstract: People are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, and those agents are increasingly encountering other people's agents over shared resources such as a codebase, a calendar, or a budget. When each agent acts for a different user with different goals, coordination often fails, and the group ends up worse off than if a single agent had acted for everyone. We study this multi-user, multi-agent setting across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: an API key environment in which agents share a compute budget, a clinic in which they share a calendar, a personal assistant environment in which they share a group order or booking, and a merge queue in which they share a release cutoff. In each scenario, we compare a single agent that serves every user (a coordinator) to a team in which each agent serves one user, with and without a communication channel between the agents. Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment: without a channel, they completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. For example, in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams. We identify distinct behaviors associated with this poor group-level performance, including stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims. We find effective but environment-specific mitigations, such as a team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and a platform check that makes an agent read its peers' messages before committing. We will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.18150.title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2611.18150.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

However, existing multi-agent collaboration leaves this loop open: collaboration is pre-defined at the operator level, topology-only learning keeps verbatim exchange that propagates errors, and reward maximization on a system's own outcomes concentrates on a few teams. To address these challenges, we propose CollabFlow, an RSI system of Learned Agent Collaboration: a trainable Collab-Director constructs teams of complete Agents, a frozen executor runs them, and each round's outcomes retrain the director.
